title: The sower explained (Matthew 13:1–23)
hook: same words, different hearers: why one sentence sticks and another vanishes
tomorrow: what happens if you pull the weeds too soon?

segments.voice: Yesterday, family at the door and a circle drawn wider than blood: my brother and sister. Now, why some words take root.

A whole podcast on the drive, and a week later one sentence is left. A teacher says a hundred things, and one of them follows you for years. Same speaker, same words, and some stick while the rest blow away. Jesus told a story about exactly that, from a boat, to a crowd standing on the beach. A sower throws seed. Then he stops with one line: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear."
screen: `ONE SENTENCE LEFT.` → `SAME WORDS, DIFFERENT HEARERS.` → `EARS TO HEAR.`

segments.voice: Later he explains it. The seed is the same everywhere, and the sower throws it everywhere, even on the path. What changes is the ground. The path is the one who "heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not," and it's snatched away. The stony ground takes it with joy, with no root, and trouble ends it. Among the thorns, "the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word." Then the good ground: "he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit." So the question is why words take root, and the answer is two verbs: hear, and understand, until it grows into something. A neighbor tradition says something close. In the Mishnah, in the collection called Pirkei Avot, a teacher named Shimon, son of Rabban Gamaliel, says in effect that the study isn't the main thing; the doing is. Jewish and Christian teachers both say the hearing has to turn into a life. And the honest difference: Pirkei Avot is speaking of Torah, God's teaching to Israel, studied and lived; Jesus' parable speaks of the word of the kingdom he is preaching. One more thing in the parable: even the good ground yields some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. No contest. Only the question: is anything taking root?
screen: `SAME SEED, DIFFERENT GROUND.` · `HEAR, AND UNDERSTAND.` · `A NEIGHBOR: NOT STUDY, BUT DEED.` · `THIRTY IS STILL GOOD GROUND.`

segments.voice: Write one sentence you've heard this week that you want to keep, by hand, on paper or a sticky note. Under it, write what it would look like done, one small thing, before tomorrow. Look at the two lines while you breathe.
The sower explained. Jesus' own reading of his story: one seed, four grounds, and the ground that understands bears fruit.
Your line: hear and understand. Then let it grow into something you do. Day done.

howItsDone: Some Christians read a short passage slowly, more than once, and stop on one phrase to carry through the day, a practice called lectio divina; some Jewish communities study Pirkei Avot on Sabbath afternoons in the weeks after Passover.

chat.says: Lena said yes to lunch! her family has a line: 'not the study, the doing.' same as the sower?
options: Close cousins: both say hearing has to bear fruit. Avot means Torah lived; the sower, the kingdom's word.
Exactly the same teaching in other words, since every religion is really saying this one thing.
Opposites: Jesus says hearing is enough, and her family's line says only the doing counts.
chat.meaning: Pirkei Avot 1:17 puts the doing first; Matthew 13:23 says the one who hears and understands bears fruit. Shared ground, different settings.

notes: Unity thread (wisdom day): Pirkei Avot 1:17 is paraphrased ('the study isn't the main thing; the doing is'), with no quotation marks, and credited to Shimon son of Rabban Gamaliel. Please have a Jewish reviewer confirm the attribution, the paraphrase, and that 'Torah, God's teaching to Israel, studied and lived' is a fair one-line description. The honest difference (Torah vs. the word of the kingdom) is stated without ranking. The rabbinic debate over whether study or deed is greater (Kiddushin 40b) is deliberately left out.
'Jewish and Christian teachers both say the hearing has to turn into a life' is a soft generalization supported by the two texts cited; confirm.

Gloss for Torah ('first, the five books of Moses'): confirm wording. Gloss for Rabban Gamaliel is kept general ('a leading Jewish teacher') because more than one Gamaliel is known; confirm which Gamaliel is meant in 1:17.
howItsDone: Pirkei Avot is studied on Sabbath afternoons between Passover and Shavuot in some communities; the text says 'some'. Confirm or cut.
13:10–17 (why he speaks in parables) is left out for length.
Greek συνίημι given in lemma form; 13:23 has συνιείς. Confirm spelling and sound-out.
